rv.q: Happily, this revival starring Alastair Whatley, which arrives in London fresh from a few months’ touring, turns out to be neither cynical nor basement-bound.
Thought-provoking, deeply moving and magnificently performed, The Importance of Being Oscar is theatre at its most intimate and affecting.
A collector’s item for Wilde connoisseurs and a moderately entertaining evening for everyone else.
Alastair Whatley's efforts to recreate the one-man review at the Park Theatre is clearly a labour of love but proves a mixed, and not entirely satisfactory bag.
For all the intelligence in Mac Liammóir’s writing, the material feels curiously remote from the wit and flamboyance of its subject.
The Importance of Being Oscar is incredibly touching and unfortunately still current and important in today’s shifting climate.
Alastair Whatley delivers a compelling performance that never lets your attention wander and fully does justice to this theatrical classic.
Whatley’s performance (supported by an excellent minimalist set and lighting) is near perfect.
The Importance of Being Oscar is the definitive account of the downfall of a great man, and deserves to be seen, especially when approached as intelligently and carefully as it is in this production.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this scholarly one-man portrait of Oscar Wilde. While some praise Whatley's engaging performance and the poignant tribute to Wilde's genius, others find it overly earnest and restrained, lacking the wit expected from its subject.
